name: Luke
title: The Gospel of Luke
iconGap: the shared pool and Luke's own Feast-cycle harvest (2026-09-25c) have both been searched against all 152 passages, and four gaps those searches called empty (Nain, the widow's mites, the woman bowed together, the dropsy) were found on 2026-11-01e by matching category names and viewing Monreale file by file, which title searches had missed, and four more on 2026-11-01f (the rich fool and the rich man and Lazarus in the Rila Monastery murals, the shepherds in the Lagoudera Nativity, Christ reading at Nazareth in the Peribleptos at Ohrid), from programmes the harvest had named under categories that pooled almost none of their files; what is left was not found in the Orthodox programmes this project has enumerated — some of it (a few of Luke's parables and miracles, some Passion moments) may simply not exist as a distinct Orthodox icon, and some may be findable in a source not yet searched (see HANDOFF Next for what was tried). Christ at twelve years had its own note: the one candidate found then is catalogued as a Mid-Pentecost icon, and the owner chose (2026-09-25e) not to use it — see HANDOFF Gotchas. Six more (the barren fig tree, the prodigal son, Zacchaeus, the sinful woman, Martha serving, the blessing of the children) were found on 2026-11-02 in the eleventh-century Paris Gospel book grec 74, whose strips sit inside the Gospel text; and two more (Christ at twelve years among the doctors, lettered with Luke's own words and painting Joseph and his mother, and the rich ruler) the same day in the ninth-century Paris Gregory, grec 510
catenaShort: Quoted verbatim from the Church Fathers venerated in the Orthodox Church — chiefly St John Chrysostom, St Cyril of Alexandria and Blessed Theophylact of Ohrid. Each quotation above names its own Father and the homily or work it is drawn from.
catenaLong: The patristic commentary quoted throughout is drawn from the Church Fathers venerated in the Orthodox Church, led by St John Chrysostom, St Cyril of Alexandria — whose commentary on St Luke survives largely in the Syriac — and Blessed Theophylact of Ohrid, whose commentary on the Gospels is the standard Orthodox reading of them, then St Ambrose and others — quoted verbatim, nothing paraphrased and nothing invented; each quotation names its own Father and the homily or work it comes from. The Carolingians, the medieval Glossa, Origen and Eusebius are excluded throughout, as in the other readers.
